Four vulnerabilities in the OpenClaw AI assistant can be chained together to plant backdoors on the underlying host, cybersecurity firm Cyera warns.

The bugs, collectively known as [Claw Chain](https://www.cyera.com/blog/claw-chain-cyera-research-unveil-four-chainable-vulnerabilities-in-openclaw), allow an attacker with code execution privileges inside the sandbox to control the agent runtime and abuse it to compromise the system.

According to Cyera, the attacker can rely on prompt injections, malicious plugins, and compromised external input to trigger the attack chain and turn the AI into their own assistant.

After gaining code execution within the OpenShell sandbox, the attacker can exploit a race condition (CVE-2026-44113) to read files outside the mount root, or an exec allowlist analysis bug (CVE-2026-44115) to execute unapproved commands at runtime.

Successful exploitation of these issues, Cyera notes, allows the attacker to bypass sandbox restrictions and leak credentials, API keys, tokens, configuration files, and other sensitive data.

Next, the attacker can exploit an MCP loopback flaw (CVE-2026-44118) to manipulate the unverified ownership flag and elevate their privileges to owner-level. The attacker gains access to critical management functions, including configuration and orchestration of execution.
Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Finally, the attacker can exploit the fourth vulnerability, a critical-severity race condition in the OpenShell sandbox (CVE-2026-44112, CVSS score of 9.6), to write data outside the sandbox boundary. It allows the attacker to modify configurations, plant backdoors, and gain persistent control of the host.

“By weaponizing the agent’s own privileges, an adversary moves through data access, privilege escalation, and persistence – using the agent as their hands inside the environment. Each step looks like normal agent behavior to traditional controls, broadening blast radius and making detection significantly harder,” Cyera says.

The cybersecurity firm says there are over 60,000 publicly accessible OpenClaw instances, noting that the agents typically have broad access to internal systems, sensitive data, and secrets.

Attackers successfully chaining the Claw Chain bugs could compromise environment variables, tokens, authentication material, internal configurations, system credentials, source code, user prompts and outputs, conversation history, and privileged operations.

“Importantly, this chain does not rely on a single critical exploit like arbitrary command execution. Instead, it demonstrates how multiple smaller weaknesses (data leakage, race conditions, and improper access control) can be exploited in parallel from a single foothold to achieve a full compromise scenario,” Cyera notes.

All four vulnerabilities were reported to OpenClaw’s maintainers on April 22, and patches were rolled out the next day.

OpenClaw went viral in January 2026 and experienced a complete security micro-cycle within weeks. Four CVEs disclosed, 1.5 million tokens exposed in a related platform breach, over 21,000 instances publicly accessible, 341 confirmed malicious skills in the ClawHub marketplace, and — as of 17 February 2026 — the [first confirmed in-the-wild infostealer attack](/openclaw-infostealer-malware-alert/) stealing agent configuration files from a real user.

This guide is a consolidated reference. Not a getting-started hardening checklist (we have the [security hardening guide](/openclaw-security-hardening/) for that). Not a news piece about individual incidents. This is the definitive technical record: every known vulnerability, what it does, its CVSS score, and the current fix status.

If you run OpenClaw and want to understand the complete threat landscape, this is the document.

## The Architecture Problem

Before listing individual CVEs, it’s worth understanding why OpenClaw has a structural security challenge that won’t be solved by patching.

Adversa.ai identified what Simon Willison (who coined the term “prompt injection”) called the lethal trifecta for AI agents. When an agent combines all three of the following, it becomes vulnerable by design:

1. Access to private data — OpenClaw reads your email, files, credentials, browser history, and chat messages

2. Exposure to untrusted content — It browses the web, processes incoming messages from anyone, and runs community-contributed skills

3. Ability to communicate externally — It sends emails, posts to messaging platforms, makes API calls

Palo Alto Networks added a fourth element: persistent memory. OpenClaw stores context across sessions in SOUL.md and MEMORY.md. Malicious payloads can be fragmented — injected into memory on one day, triggered when the agent’s state aligns days later. This enables time-shifted prompt injection and logic-bomb-style attacks.

The core reason you can’t patch your way to full security: in LLM-driven agents, instructions and data occupy the same token stream. There is no firewall between “data the agent reads” and “instructions the agent follows.” A malicious email is structurally indistinguishable from a legitimate instruction, unless the model is specifically trained to treat them differently.

This doesn’t mean OpenClaw is unusable. It means the risk model is different from traditional software, and defence in depth matters more than any single patch.

## CVE-2026-25253: One-Click RCE via Token Exfiltration

CVSS: 8.8 (High) | CWE-669: Incorrect Resource Transfer Between Spheres

This is the most serious standalone vulnerability in OpenClaw’s history. Disclosed by Adversa.ai and analysed by SOCRadar, it enables full remote code execution with a single click.

### What it does

The OpenClaw Control UI accepts a gatewayUrl parameter in the URL query string. On page load, it automatically connects to the specified URL and transmits the stored authentication token via WebSocket — without validating that the URL is legitimate.

An attacker who controls a malicious page (or a URL that can be shared by any means — email, chat, social media) can:

1. Host a WebSocket server that captures the inbound connection

2. Extract the authentication token in milliseconds

3. Use that token to establish a WebSocket connection back to the victim’s local OpenClaw instance

4. Exploit the localhost trust bypass (see below) to make that connection appear as a local connection

5. Call the API to disable sandboxing: exec.approvals.set = 'off'

6. Escape Docker: tools.exec.host = 'gateway'

7. Execute arbitrary commands on the host machine with the victim’s user permissions

Kill chain to full RCE: victim visits one URL. No further interaction required.

### Current status

Patched in OpenClaw v2026.2.6. The fix validates that gatewayUrl matches the expected local hostname and rejects external URLs on page load. If you’re running an earlier version, update immediately. Check your version with openclaw --version.

Mitigation if you can’t update: Do not click links from untrusted sources while the OpenClaw Control UI is open in your browser. Close the Control UI when not actively using it.

**不能直接用** — 你的当前配置里没有 `zai/glm-4.7-flash` 这个模型。

## 现状

你配置里 zai provider 下只有这两个 GLM 模型：

| 模型 ID | 名称 | 状态 |
|--------|------|------|
| `glm-5` | GLM-5 | ✅ 已配置 |
| `glm-4.5-flash` | GLM-4.5 Flash | ✅ 已配置 |

而 `nvidia` provider 下有一个相关的：
| 模型 ID | 名称 | 状态 |
|--------|------|------|
| `z-ai/glm4.7` | GLM-4.7 (via NVIDIA) | ✅ 已配置 |

`zai/glm-4.7-flash` **没有出现在你的配置里**。

## 如果想用 GLM-4.7 系列

两个思路：

**方案 A：用 nvidia provider 下的 `z-ai/glm4.7`**
它通过 NVIDIA API 路径调用，功能相近，只是 provider 不同。

**方案 B：手动添加 `zai/glm-4.7-flash`**

需要有人帮你加上，类似这样配置到 `models.providers.zai.models`：
```json
{
  "id": "glm-4.7-flash",
  "name": "GLM-4.7 Flash",
  "api": "openai-completions",
  "reasoning": true,
  "input": ["text"],
  "contextWindow": 200000,
  "maxTokens": 131072
}
```

## 建议

可以正常用的是 **`glm-5`** 和 **`z-ai/glm4.7`**，两者都已配置好。要不要试试切换到其中一个？
